沙槌屬體鳴樂器，起源於前哥倫布時期，與南美洲和加勒比海原住民的儀式及溝通用途有關: The maraca is an idiophone, dating from before Columbus and connected with ritual and communication among the indigenous peoples of South America and the Caribbean; ethnographic accounts attribute its invention to peoples such as the Arawak and the Taíno. In the eighteenth century the Jesuit missionary José Gumilla recorded maracas used by Arawak-speaking peoples of the Orinoco basin. It is also traced to Colombia in South America, where it is more than 1,500 years old, and similar ancient evidence is found in Jamaica, Venezuela, Cuba and Trinidad. Modern shells use leather, wood, plastic or metal, and plastic pellets, metal shot or beans replace the seeds inside.

In Latin American popular music it is associated with genres such as the Cuban son, guaracha, danzón, salsa, bomba, mambo, samba, cumbia and calypso. In an ensemble it is usually played in pairs, though some styles, such as bomba, use a single one. Examples to listen to include No. 2 of the Carmen Suite by Shchedrin/Bizet, the seventh movement of Prokofiev's 'Alexander Nevsky', and several of Arturo Márquez's danzones.

Measurements show its frequency response at roughly 3,000 to 10,000 Hz. Volume and timbre are affected by the shell material and by what is inside. Compared with the shekere, the maraca's impact sound comes mainly from inside the container, while the shekere, with its net of sounding bodies on the outside, sounds mainly from without.

The maraca is a struck idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 112.13, common in Caribbean and Latin American music and occasionally in rock. It is a container holding seeds, plastic pellets, metal shot or beans, joined to a handle and shaken with the wrist so that the contents strike the wall and make the sound; it is usually played in pairs, though a single one can be used. Ancient ones were mostly made from fruits such as gourds or calabashes, and today plastic, metal or leather are also used. Beside rhythmic accompaniment, it also appears in indigenous and Afro-Brazilian ritual, healing and dance settings.
演奏沙槌時，一手或兩手持握柄，盡量不觸及球體發聲部。球體朝上向外，約成三十至四十: To play the maraca, hold the handle with one hand or both, touching the sounding part of the head as little as possible. The head points up and outwards, at about thirty to forty-five degrees. The sound comes from turning the wrist outwards to shake the instrument so that the seeds, pellets or metal shot strike the shell. A beginner can first practise a steady rhythm with one, then shaking a pair together; some styles use only one, others require a pair.
